title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in California, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "CA"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

county_data <- get_acs(

Let’s look at what came back.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California        1181   705   59.7 
 2 Trinity County, California        922   220   23.9 
 3 Plumas County, California        1034   148   14.3 
 4 Mono County, California          1593   212   13.3 
 5 Mariposa County, California      1268   165   13.0 
 6 Calaveras County, California     1615   142    8.79
 7 Modoc County, California          818    71    8.68
 8 Lake County, California          1292   110    8.51
 9 Tuolumne County, California      1247   103    8.26
10 Inyo County, California          1140    88    7.72


The county with the largest margin of error is Sierra County, with a margin of error equal to 59.7% of its estimate.

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    39

There are 39 counties in the high-confidence category, 13 in moderate, and 6 in low confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     2318     17 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California        NA     NA    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      1380    106   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       1369     31  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   1615    142   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1139     67   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         39        989118.
2 Low confidence           3          6771.
3 Moderate                16         40430.


High-confidence counties have an average population of about 989117.821, while low-confidence counties have an average population of about 6770.667. This confirms that smaller counties tend to have less reliable data.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
In this analysis, I found that we know the least about small, rural counties in California. For example, Sierra County has a margin of error equal to 59.7% of its median gross rent estimate, meaning we cannot confidently say what the actual rent is. Trinity and Plumas counties also have high margins of error, above 14%. This pattern exists because the American Community Survey is a sample, not a full count. Smaller populations produce smaller sample sizes, which naturally result in greater statistical uncertainty. If a state agency allocated rental assistance funding using this data and ignored the margins of error, smaller counties like Sierra, Trinity, and Plumas could be severely hurt. Because their estimates are unreliable, they might be overlooked entirely, receiving far less funding than they actually need. This would exacerbate existing inequalities between urban and rural areas. Thus, ignoring uncertainty in ACS data can lead to inequitable policy outcomes, prioritizing well-measured, populous counties over the communities we know the least about.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
The article
I am using Option A, the provided article: Alfred Lubrano, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”, WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018.
It compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims:

Citywide poverty stood at 26 percent.
Fairhill had a 61 percent poverty rate.
Eastwick jumped from 12 to 26 percent, the largest rise of any neighborhood.
Holmesburg rose from 2 to 19 percent; Mayfair from 1 to 14 percent.
Poverty rose in 22 majority-white neighborhoods.

Census tracts are not neighborhoods, and the article never published which tracts went into which neighborhood, so I work at the tract level for Philadelphia County. My numbers will not match the article’s exactly — that is expected, not a failure.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct the data
I pull table B17001 at the tract level: B17001_002 (population below the poverty level) over B17001_001 (population for whom poverty status is determined). A poverty rate needs a numerator and a denominator, and its margin of error has to be propagated from both with moe_prop() — it does not carry over from the count. I use survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 (the 2006–2010 window) and year = 2017 (2013–2017), the two periods the article names, because tract-level estimates only exist in the 5-year ACS and the article says it used the five-year figures.
The article forces a few assumptions on me: it publishes no tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, so tract level is as far as I can go; Philadelphia County (state 42, county 101) matches the city boundary; tracts are matched across periods by GEOID; and any tract with a zero or missing denominator gets NA instead of an invalid rate. The two windows share no calendar years, so the two estimates are independent, and the standard MOE for a difference — sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²) — is exactly right here. If the windows overlapped, the estimates would be positively correlated and that formula would overstate the MOE of the change.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  below_poverty = "B17001_002",
  total         = "B17001_001"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  state  = 42,
  county = 101,
  year   = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

n_distinct(acs_2010$GEOID)


[1] 384


Show code
n_distinct(acs_2017$GEOID)


[1] 384


Both periods return 384 tracts.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 2: Test the change
For each tract and period I compute the poverty rate and its MOE with moe_prop(), setting the rate to NA wherever the denominator is zero or missing.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_2017 <- acs_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013_2017",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


Each ACS MOE is at 90 percent confidence, so the standard error is MOE / 1.645. The change is the difference of the two rates, its MOE is sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²), and the change counts as statistically detectable when the z-score clears the 90 percent critical value of 1.645. I also compute each estimate’s coefficient of variation (SE / estimate × 100) and flag reliability with the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12 reliable, 12–40 somewhat reliable, > 40 unreliable.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    )
  )


Eight tracts come back NA. Before deciding what to do with them, I checked why.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(is.na(change)) %>%
  left_join(acs_2010 %>% select(GEOID, total_2010 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  left_join(acs_2017 %>% select(GEOID, total_2017 = totalE), by = "GEOID") %>%
  select(NAME, total_2010, total_2017)


# A tibble: 8 × 3
  NAME                                                 total_2010 total_2017
  <chr>                                                     <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Census Tract 50, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania            0          0
2 Census Tract 9803, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0
3 Census Tract 9804, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0
4 Census Tract 9805, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0
5 Census Tract 9806, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania         92          0
6 Census Tract 9807, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0
7 Census Tract 9808, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0
8 Census Tract 9809, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania          0          0


All eight are zero-population special-use tracts — Tract 50 plus the 9800-series (9803–9809), which in Philadelphia cover institutional and non-residential land such as the airport. Their population with poverty status determined is zero in both periods, so a poverty rate is undefined, not merely noisy. I exclude them and test the remaining 376.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  summarise(
    total_tracts    = n(),
    excluded_na     = sum(is.na(significant)),
    detectable      = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detectable  = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    detectable_up   = sum(significant & change > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    detectable_down = sum(significant & change < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 6
  total_tracts excluded_na detectable not_detectable detectable_up
         <int>       <int>      <int>          <int>         <int>
1          384           8         63            313            36
# ℹ 1 more variable: detectable_down <int>


Show code
poverty_complete <- poverty_tested %>%
  filter(!is.na(change), !is.na(moe_diff), se_diff > 0)

poverty_complete %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rate_2006_2010 = mean(poverty_rate_2006_2010) * 100,
    avg_rate_2013_2017 = mean(poverty_rate_2013_2017) * 100,
    median_change_pp   = median(change) * 100,
    tracts_over_55pct_2017 = sum(poverty_rate_2013_2017 > 0.55)
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  avg_rate_2006_2010 avg_rate_2013_2017 median_change_pp tracts_over_55pct_2017
               <dbl>              <dbl>            <dbl>                  <int>
1               25.5               26.1             1.15                     22


Of 376 testable tracts, only 63 (17 percent) show a change distinguishable from zero at 90 percent confidence — 36 up, 27 down. The other 313 (83 percent) could easily not have changed at all.
The average tract poverty rate did drift up, from 25.5 to 26.1 percent — which squares with the article’s citywide “26 percent” — and 22 tracts still sit above 55 percent, so the concentrated, Fairhill-style poverty the article describes is real. But a city where five tracts in six show no detectable change is mostly flat, not surging. One artifact needs a flag: the largest single “decrease” is special-use Tract 9800 (about 84 → 5 percent, group-quarters population), and special-use tracts 9891 and 9801 carry MOEs of ±221 and ±163 points, so the error-bar plot below clips its axis.

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
The evidence
First, the required error-bar view: every tract’s change with its 90 percent MOE, ordered from largest decrease to largest increase, with zero marked. A tract only counts as changed when its whiskers clear zero.


Show code
poverty_complete %>%
  mutate(
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_pp    = moe_diff * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(change_pp) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = change_pp, color = significant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_pp, ymax = change_pp + moe_pp),
    fatten = 0.5
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-60, 70)) +
  scale_color_discrete(
    labels = c("Not detectable", "Detectable at 90% conf.")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Philadelphia tracts show no detectable poverty change",
    subtitle = "376 tracts ordered by estimated change; whiskers are 90% MOE of the change.
                Axis clipped at -60/+70 points (two special-use tracts' MOEs exceed +/-160).",
    x = "Census tracts, ordered by estimated change",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    color = NULL
  )









For the grey majority, the error bar swallows the estimate. Some MOEs are more than a hundred times the estimated change itself (Tract 306: −0.03 ± 8.3 points).
Next, the reliability table: the 15 largest statistically detectable increases, with each period’s CV colored by the Jurjevich thresholds. This is exactly the population of tracts an article like this one quotes from.


Show code
poverty_tested %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant), significant, change > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(change)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  transmute(
    tract          = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    rate_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    rate_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    change_pp      = change * 100,
    moe_pp         = moe_diff * 100,
    cv_2006_2010,
    cv_2013_2017
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "The 15 largest detectable poverty-rate increases") %>%
  cols_label(
    tract          = "Tract",
    rate_2006_2010 = "Rate 06–10 (%)",
    rate_2013_2017 = "Rate 13–17 (%)",
    change_pp      = "Change (pp)",
    moe_pp         = "± MOE (pp)",
    cv_2006_2010   = "CV 06–10",
    cv_2013_2017   = "CV 13–17"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(rate_2006_2010, rate_2013_2017, change_pp, moe_pp,
                cv_2006_2010, cv_2013_2017),
    decimals = 1
  ) %>%
  data_color(
    columns = c(cv_2006_2010, cv_2013_2017),
    fn = function(x) case_when(
      x < 12  ~ "#C6EFCE",
      x <= 40 ~ "#FFEB9C",
      TRUE    ~ "#FFC7CE"
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "CV thresholds per Jurjevich et al. (2018): green = CV < 12% (reliable),
     amber = 12–40% (somewhat reliable), red = > 40% (unreliable).

title: Verify the Claim: poverty and inequality in Philadelphia neighborhoods
text:
Part 4: Rewrite the central paragraph
New five-year Census estimates paint a sobering but more nuanced picture of Philadelphia. Averaged across the city’s 384 census tracts, the poverty rate in 2013–2017 was about 26 percent, up modestly from 2006–2010. The average hides extremes: in more than 20 tracts, poverty exceeds 55 percent — echoing the deprivation reported in Fairhill — and eight tracts saw statistically confirmed increases of 20 percentage points or more. Yet most of the city did not measurably move: in 313 of 376 testable tracts, the change was too small to distinguish from sampling error. Because the American Community Survey is a sample, small-area figures carry wide margins of error — especially where poverty is rare — so dramatic neighborhood-level jumps deserve skepticism before they are believed.

The article
I am using Option A, the provided article: Alfred Lubrano, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”, WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer, December 6, 2018.
It compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates and makes several specific claims:

Fairhill had a 61 percent poverty rate.
Eastwick jumped from 12 to 26 percent, the largest rise of any neighborhood.
Holmesburg rose from 2 to 19 percent; Mayfair from 1 to 14 percent.
Poverty rose in 22 majority-white neighborhoods.

Census tracts are not neighborhoods, and the article never published which tracts went into which neighborhood, so I work at the tract level for Philadelphia County. My numbers will not match the article’s exactly — that is expected, not a failure.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 1: Reconstruct the data
For poverty, I use ACS table B17001: B17001_002 (people below the poverty level) as the numerator and B17001_001 (people for whom poverty status is determined) as the denominator. A poverty rate is a proportion, so its margin of error must be derived from both the numerator and the denominator using moe_prop() — the MOE of the count does not carry over to the rate. I use survey = "acs5" for year = 2010 (the 2006–2010 window) and year = 2017 (the 2013–2017 window), the two periods the article compares, because tract-level data are only available in the 5-year ACS and the article states it used five-year estimates.
Because the article does not publish its methods, I have to make several assumptions: there is no public tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, so I stay at the tract level; Philadelphia County (state 42, county 101) corresponds to the city boundary; tracts are linked across periods by GEOID; and any tract with a zero or missing denominator is set to NA rather than producing an invalid rate. The two windows do not share any calendar years, so the two estimates are independent. That makes the standard formula for the MOE of a difference — sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²) — appropriate. If the windows overlapped, the estimates would be positively correlated, and this formula would overstate the MOE of the change.

text:
Part 2: Test the change
For each tract and period I compute the poverty rate and its MOE with moe_prop(), setting the rate to NA wherever the denominator is zero or missing.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- acs_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006_2010",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_2017 <- acs_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013_2017",
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate     = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate, NA_real_),
    poverty_rate_moe = if_else(totalE > 0, poverty_rate_moe, NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)

poverty_wide <- bind_rows(poverty_2010, poverty_2017) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


Each ACS MOE is at 90 percent confidence, so the standard error is MOE / 1.645. The change is the difference of the two rates, its MOE is sqrt(MOE1² + MOE2²), and the change counts as statistically detectable when the z-score clears the 90 percent critical value of 1.645. I also compute each estimate’s coefficient of variation (SE / estimate × 100) and flag reliability with the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12 reliable, 12–40 somewhat reliable, > 40 unreliable.


Show code

  mutate(
    change   = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    se_1     = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2     = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cv_2006_2010 = se_1 / poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,
    cv_2013_2017 = se_2 / poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017) ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12   ~ "reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40  ~ "somewhat reliable",

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    n_septa  = lengths(st_intersects(., layer2)),
    n_indego = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1))
  )

summary(tracts$n_septa)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   4.00   17.75   28.00   35.13   46.00  183.00 


Code
summary(tracts$n_indego)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  0.0000  0.0000  0.7789  1.0000  7.0000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
mutate(
    area_sqmi       = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    septa_per_sqmi  = n_septa / area_sqmi,
    indego_per_sqmi = n_indego / area_sqmi
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx_indego <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer1)
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_indego_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, layer1[nearest_idx_indego, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

nearest_idx_septa <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_septa_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, layer2[nearest_idx_septa, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.

          notes = "spatial feature")

model_log <- model_log %>%

          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = septa_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(septa_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-18.5194  -3.0884  -0.0491   2.9256  16.3693 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     25.87577    0.69995  36.968  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi       2.10433    0.25419   8.279 2.19e-15 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2) -0.12422    0.01908  -6.511 2.39e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.054 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1911,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1868 
F-statistic: 44.54 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "#5A189D") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  79
2 Inner 134
3 Outer 167


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5146  -3.2886  -0.1537   3.1284  17.1430 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  27.5537     0.5699  48.349  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner     4.3575     0.7185   6.065 3.21e-09 ***
ringOuter     6.4529     0.6917   9.329  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.065 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1833 
F-statistic: 43.52 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: 1. What helped, and what didn’t? The squared distance to City Hall helped the most, lowering CV RMSE from 5.22 to 5.03. It captured the non-linear decay of commute times as you move away from the urban core. SEPTA density and Indego distance disappointed—they slightly worsened CV RMSE. This is likely because they measure infrastructure presence rather than actual travel speed, and they overlap with the central-city variables already in the model.

Read one coefficient twice. For I(dist_ch_mi^2), the β̂ reading is that for every additional squared mile from City Hall, predicted commute time decreases by about 0.062 minutes, reflecting the diminishing effect of distance. The ŷ reading is that this quadratic term lets the model bend, which improves its ability to predict commutes in outer tracts where the distance effect flattens out.
What’s still missing? Looking at the final residual map, orange clusters remain in Northeast Philadelphia. I would want to measure distance to the nearest highway on-ramp or regional rail station. These capture actual commuting speed and mode choice, which the current model lacks.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? The fog plot shows a clear upward trend: tracts with higher CV in their commute-time estimate also tend to have larger model errors. This suggests that a substantial share of the remaining error is ACS sampling noise rather than model failure, especially in smaller or more variable tracts. —
